**Short-video recommendation learns from behavior that is easy to misread.** A completed five-second clip and a completed five-minute video do not indicate identical preference. A replay may mean delight or confusion; a long dwell may reflect distraction. Define satisfaction using several signals rather than equating one event with user benefit.

**Use a multi-stage funnel.** Retrieve candidates from followed creators, similar content, collaborative history, and exploration pools. A ranker uses richer user–item features on that shortlist. A final stage handles repetition, diversity, eligibility, and policy constraints. Different stages have different latency and modeling budgets.

**Why exploration is necessary.** If the system only displays what its current model already believes the user likes, it collects little evidence about new interests or creators. Controlled exploration supplies information, but should be bounded by product constraints and evaluated for user experience. Logging the selection mechanism makes later analysis more interpretable. [4](https://research.google/pubs/sampling-bias-corrected-neural-modeling-for-large-corpus-item-recommendations/)

**An example of a feedback loop.** A user pauses on one cooking clip; the model fills the next page with cooking videos; subsequent cooking engagement appears to confirm a strong exclusive preference. Some of that signal was created by the system's own narrow exposure. Diverse candidate pools and long-term evaluation help distinguish discovery from self-reinforcement.

Measure skips, retained engagement, explicit negative feedback, creator/item coverage, and longer-term satisfaction. Compare by user and content slices. A gain in immediate watch time may come with fatigue or repetitive recommendations, so a successful ranking experiment needs guardrails beyond a single aggregate engagement metric.

**Technical details and references.**

Use a multi-stage funnel: candidate pools from followed creators, content similarity, collaborative retrieval, and controlled exploration; a ranking stage predicts satisfaction signals; a final layer enforces diversity, safety, and repetition limits. Capture swipe, dwell, completion, replay, explicit feedback, and exposure position with reliable event IDs.

A streaming feature path updates session state after each interaction, allowing the last few swipes to change ranking. Handle event-time ordering, duplicate events, late arrivals, and feature freshness; the request can also carry its latest confirmed actions to bridge stream lag. Keep persistent interests and short-session interests distinct.

Watch time favors longer videos, while completion favors shorter ones. Model multiple outcomes and normalize/segment by length; optimize a validated satisfaction objective with negative-feedback and retention guardrails. Do not interpret every rapid swipe identically. Evaluate session satisfaction, creator diversity, repeats, harmful exposure, and long-term retention. A stale-stream fallback uses durable user features and safe popular candidates rather than blocking the feed.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** A multi-objective score might combine expected satisfaction, completion, and negative-feedback costs, but weights encode product tradeoffs rather than universal constants. Use long-term holdouts to detect novelty effects and feedback loops. Diversity constraints and exploration preserve coverage; training only on previous top-ranked impressions can reinforce a narrow view of user preference. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.06978)
